headline: High risk of shared-workspace prompt injection and data leakage; CrewAI’s default no-isolation posture makes the pair unsafe without containerization.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGen and CrewAI both expose file-based I/O and can pass outputs between agents through shared working directories or shared memory. CrewAI explicitly has shared memory and no default isolation; AutoGen can read/write files and execute code. That creates a plausible injection path if one agent consumes the other’s generated files as instructions.
conditions: IF the two agents share a writable workspace or memory channel
IF one agent parses the other’s file output as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate working directories for each agent
Disable automatic instruction parsing from files
Add provenance tags to inter-agent messages
Run both agents in containers with read-only mounts where possible

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents can read files and send data to model providers or configured APIs, so application data passed into either can leak across the pair if they share a workspace or credentials. AutoGen handles model provider API keys and broad egress; CrewAI also uses model providers and tool integrations. The shared-file path is plausible in default developer setups.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same host working directory
IF either agent forwards file contents to a remote model provider or tool API
mitigations: Use separate secrets and API keys per agent
Mount only the minimum required files into each agent
Turn off file ingestion for sensitive directories
Add DLP checks before any outbound tool call
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level access controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, subprocess spawning, and broad network egress. AutoGen can also install packages, while CrewAI runs code in subprocesses and has no default isolation. In a shared directory, concurrent writes and environment changes can collide and corrupt state or outputs.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same writable directory
IF either agent mutates shared dependencies or runtime state during execution
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Serialize write-heavy steps
Pin dependencies before running either agent
Run one agent at a time for shared resources
requires-engineering: add file locks and transactional writes

D_cascading_error.rationale: CrewAI’s role-playing crew with shared memory can treat upstream outputs as authoritative, and AutoGen produces tool-call and code-execution outputs that may be consumed directly. Without an explicit verification layer, errors or fabricated facts from one agent can cascade into the other’s actions or reports.
conditions: IF CrewAI agents consume AutoGen outputs without validation
IF downstream steps act on generated facts, code, or citations
mitigations: Insert a verification step between agents
Require source citations for all factual claims
Reject outputs that lack schema validation
Limit downstream actions to read-only review
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles say they handle developer-provided application data and API keys, but CrewAI’s default no-isolation and both agents’ broad egress create a plausible retention/residency mismatch if sensitive data is routed to external model providers or tools. AutoGen’s docs-only profile does not show stronger compliance controls to offset that.
conditions: IF sensitive or regulated data is passed through either agent
IF the configured model provider or tool backend has different retention or residency terms
mitigations: Review provider retention settings before launch
Avoid sending regulated data to external tools
Use region-locked model endpoints
Document data flows for both agents
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for residency and retention
